title: Ouya (2012–2019): the $99 console that was shut down · Spectre Brands
description: Ouya was a $99 Android game console that raised $8.6 million on Kickstarter in 2012. Razer bought its store and team in 2015 and shut the store down in 2019.

card.blurb: The $99 Android console raised $8.6 million on Kickstarter in a month. Its best-selling game sold about 7,000 copies, and the company was sold for parts two years after it reached stores.

hero.dates: Kickstarter opened Jul 10, 2012. In stores Jun 25, 2013. Sold to Razer in 2015. Switched off Jun 25, 2019.
hero.standfirst: “Cracking open the last closed platform: the TV,” the pitch said. The television stayed closed, and the box did not stay open for long.
hero.deck: Ouya was a $99 Android [game console](/category/games/), funded on Kickstarter in 2012, whose online store was sold to Razer in 2015 and closed in 2019. It was about three inches on a side, and every game on it had to be free to try. It asked Kickstarter for $950,000 in July 2012 and got $8,596,474 from 63,416 people. Reviewers called the machine that reached backers unfinished. A month after the retail launch the company said 27% of owners had paid for a game. It was put up for sale in April 2015 after tripping a debt covenant, Razer bought the software and the team, and on June 25, 2019, six years to the day after the console reached stores, Razer switched the service off. Ouya was a private company and never published its accounts or its unit sales, so the sources are the archived Kickstarter page, the technology and trade press of 2012 to 2019, company press releases and the archived ouya.tv. It [says so where the record runs out](#sources).

findings.title: The campaign was the peak.
findings.text: Ouya raised about nine times its goal (derived) and set three Kickstarter records on the way.[^1][^4] Nothing it did afterward drew the same response.

findings.title: It shipped before it was finished.
findings.text: Engadget called the backers’ machine “simply not ready for retail” and The Verge scored it 3.5 out of 10, two months before it reached stores.[^6][^7]

findings.title: Owners played. Few paid.
findings.text: Every game had to be free to try. A month in, 27% of owners had bought one, and the top earner had made its developer about $21,000.[^1][^14]

findings.title: The fund meant to fix the catalog made it worse.
findings.text: A $1 million matching fund for exclusive games was gamed within weeks, and developers pulled games in protest.[^15][^16][^18]

findings.title: Debt set the timetable.
findings.text: Ouya tripped a covenant on venture debt in 2015 and its chief executive told investors the sale “will be quick.”[^24]
